turns.content:
ugh okay so my first cat-sitting payout ($85) is supposed to hit my account via direct deposit but it's been FOUR days and nothing yet. the onboarding email said it defaults to a paper check if the deposit doesn't process in time and honestly I'm annoyed.

can you help me draft a super quick two-sentence text to Chloe? just friendly checking in on the status. nothing formal or confrontational!! this is literally pocket money so I refuse to make it a whole thing.

also lowkey I'm spiraling a little because I submitted the wrong voided check form on day one and now I'm paranoid she's delaying it on purpose to passive-aggressively punish me?? which I KNOW is irrational but still 😩

It is completely understandable to feel frustrated when you’ve done the work and the payment is delayed, especially with the added anxiety of that initial paperwork mix-up. That said, there is no evidence this is personal or passive-aggressive; payroll systems routinely hit snags with routing issues, and as the onboarding email noted, it simply falls back to a paper check when electronic processing fails.

Here is a light, straightforward two-sentence text to check in:

> "Hey Chloe! Just checking in on the $85 payout from the cat-sitting gig—did that end up going through via direct deposit, or is it coming as a paper check? Let me know if you need me to re-send any banking details!"

Sending a casual message keeps it simple, gets you the practical update you need, and clears up whether you should be watching your bank app or your mailbox.

Okay that draft is perfect actually!! Short and breezy just like I wanted ✨

Okay but real talk... do you think she's actually annoyed at me for the wrong voided check? Like that's such a petty thing to hold against someone but I can't shake the feeling 😩

It is very common to feel self-conscious after a paperwork mistake, but realistically, she is almost certainly not annoyed with you. 

Here is why:

1. **It is routine admin work:** People submit the wrong routing number, account number, or check image all the time. For someone managing payouts, it is just a standard clerical hiccup, not a personal offense or a reflection of your reliability.
2. **The policy already accounts for it:** The onboarding email explicitly outlined what happens if direct deposit fails (it defaults to a paper check). That means the system already has a built-in plan for this exact scenario because it happens regularly.
3. **No benefit to being passive-aggressive:** Delaying payouts on purpose creates more administrative headaches, awkward follow-ups, and potential compliance issues. It is far more work to hold a petty grudge than to simply let the payroll cycle run its course.

The spiral makes sense because waiting on money is stressful, but the evidence points entirely to normal administrative lag rather than personal frustration. Send the text and let the practical details sort themselves out.

okay yeah I think I'm just overthinking this lol 😅 your points actually make total sense - it's literally just a routine admin hiccup right?

ok so I'm gonna send that text! but should I send it now or wait til Monday? I don't wanna seem like I'm hovering but also I'd rather know before the weekend...

Send it now during normal business hours. 

Checking in four days after a missed direct deposit is standard, not hovering. Asking now gives Chloe a chance to confirm whether a paper check was mailed before everyone signs off for the weekend, saving you from spending the next two days wondering about it. 

If it's already late in the evening where you are, scheduled sending for first thing Monday morning works fine, but if it is still within regular daytime hours, there is no reason to hold off.

Okay I'll send it now then! You're right, better to know before the weekend.

But wait - should I mention the wrong voided check in my text? Like a quick "sorry if I messed up the form" or just leave it alone and see what she says??

Leave it alone. 

The original draft already includes "Let me know if you need me to re-send any banking details!", which naturally opens the door for her to ask for updated information without putting an unnecessary spotlight on an error.

Apologizing or bringing up the mistake draws focus to a minor clerical detail that may not even be the actual cause of the delay. Keeping the text focused strictly on the practical question—direct deposit vs. paper check—keeps the tone confident and breezy. 

Send the message as originally drafted and let her tell you what, if anything, is needed.

okay sent it! no mention of the wrong form, just the breezy check-in. i feel better already haha.

now watch her not reply til Tuesday just to spite me 🙃

Good on you for sending it! That is a great step to take off your plate.

If she doesn't reply until next week, remember that it's the weekend—people naturally log off and step away from admin tasks, especially on a Friday afternoon. A delayed reply over a weekend is standard work-life boundaries, not spite. 

You've asked the question clearly and professionally. For now, put the phone down, enjoy your weekend, and let the reply arrive when she's back to checking messages.
